newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Clinton, Jiang agree to summits, differ on WTO.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Jiang agree to summits, differ on WTO.

text.p: A breakthrough announcement that U.S. President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin will hold summits in each other's capitals gave APEC leaders a boost on Sunday on the eve of their meeting in the Philippines.

An almost decade-long top-level standoff between China and the United States has clouded efforts by the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum to forge the world's biggest free trade zone around the Pacific by 2020.
White House press secretary Mike McCurry said Clinton and Jiang accepted each other's invitations for summits in Washington and Beijing after an 85-minute private meeting.
After Clinton and Jiang had appeared before cameras, both smiling broadly, he said the session had "moved the vital (Sino-American) strategic relationship forward".
Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Shen Guofeng described the talks as "friendly, positive and constructive".
Despite the new warmth, however, the two sides remained at odds over Chinese membership of the World Trade Organisation, which sets the rules for global commerce.
Clinton told Jiang the United States looked forward to China joining, but Beijing had to make more concessions on trade liberalisation.

As Clinton and Jiang met on the fringes of the APEC conference, thousands of leftwing demonstrators piled into Manila's trademark jeepneys -- gaily-decorated minibuses styled after World War Two U.S. jeeps -- to try to drive to the summit site in Subic Bay. But the protests went into gridlock.

Leaders from 18 APEC economies, embracing nations from Papua New Guinea to Chile and Canada, are meeting to put flesh on plans to dismantle trade barriers in developing member nations by 2010 and in developed countries by 2020.
Riot police blocked one motorcade, preventing it from reaching the main highway to Subic Bay, a former U.S. naval base 80 km (50 miles) north of Manila. A second convoy stalled in the chaos.
Roman Catholic nuns among the protesters prayed with rosary beads amid chants of "let the people through".
Colourful banners streaming from the shiny jeepneys, some packed with 20 people or more, proclaimed "Junk APEC" and "Save our Natural Resources".
The People's Conference on Imperialist Globalisation, which organised one convoy, denounces APEC as a ploy by rich nations to prise open Third World markets and rape the environment.
Philippine police said they had been instructed to use "maximum tolerance" with the protesters but were determined to prevent them reaching the heavily guarded summit venue.
U.S. officials have warned that American nationals at APEC may be targets for leftist terrorist attack.
Clinton's motorcade made a last-minute switch of routes from Manila airport on Saturday night after two men were reported lurking suspiciously at a traffic light.

The U.S. President, relaxed after a five-day working holiday in Australia, had a busy schedule which also included bilateral meetings with the leaders of Japan and South Korea and APEC host nation, the Philippines.
While here, Clinton was also expected to push for support to abolish all tariffs on communication technology by 2000.
APEC ministers on Saturday urged the WTO to back the liberalisation measure in a watered-down statement following opposition from countries with misgivings over the pace and product coverage.
"Discussions are going on and it's at rather a sensitive stage," Philippines Foreign Ministry undersecretary Rodolfo Severino told a news briefing after Clinton met Philippines President Fidel Ramos.
Clinton will be the first U.S. leader to visit China since George Bush in early 1989.
Since then relations have been dogged by disputes over human rights, arms proliferation, Taiwan and trade.
Relations reached a critical point in March when China conducted missile tests during Taiwan's elections and the United States dispatched two aircraft carrier battle groups to the area in response.
U.S. First Lady Hillary Clinton was denounced on Sunday by Filipino feminists near a hotel where she was speaking.
"Hillary Clinton merely parrots pro-women concerns but in essence is a tool of imperialists," one of the protesters said before riot police scattered them.
